transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-08 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Michael Lee (Atlas - Head of ML), Priya Nair (Platform), Jordan Smith (CTO)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick agenda: we want to walk through Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix / KV cache, show a simple cost model, and outline a pilot.
[00:18] Michael: Sounds good. For context we have a production recommender that's about 120 QPS at peak, and latency SLO is 200ms p95. We're currently self-hosting with a mix of CPUs and a couple of GPUs.
[00:33] Samira: Got it. That helps. Two quick clarifying q's: are most of your calls short prompts with long context? or long prompts with short context?
[00:45] Priya: It's mixed — initial user text is short, but we attach full user history ~2k tokens. We do a lot of prefix-like prompts for personalization.
[00:58] Alex: Perfect. That's exactly the case where prefix / KV cache can help. We'll show how a high cache hit rate reduces token compute and cost, especially for repeated prefixes like history or system instructions.
[01:12] Samira: Quick note — transcription may mangle some names, so I'll call out numbers verbally too.

[01:30] Samira: So first slide, batching basics. When you increase batch size you amortize model load and token decode costs, but you also increase tail latency due to waiting for batch fill. For your 200ms p95 we recommend a mixed policy: dynamic batching with a hard latency cap ~120ms and burst mode for spikes.
[01:55] Michael: Does that mean smaller batches at p95, and larger ones at p50?
[02:05] Samira: Exactly — you can tune per-route. For recommender route, configure target batch size 8 and max batch wait 10ms as a starting point; in practice we see throughput improvements of 2-3x with minimal p95 impact.

[02:28] Alex: Now the KV / prefix cache. Two patterns: prefix cache where you store the first N tokens of the convo, and KV cache where we cache transformer KV states per prefix to skip recomputation. Both reduce token compute but KV cache tends to give larger wins for long histories.
[02:47] Jordan: Is KV cache safe for personalization? any privacy concerns?
[02:53] Samira: It's just cached model states — you can encrypt at rest and use customer KMS in Private/Dedicated. For hosted we offer tenant separation and audit logs; for regulated data you can run on Redwood Private with your KMS.

[03:12] Priya: Can you give a concrete cost example?
[03:15] Alex: Sure. Here's a simple model: baseline token compute cost for full decode = $X per 1k tokens (for example numbers today assume $2.50 per 1M tokens for the model family). If you have a 70% KV hit rate on prefixes that represent 40% of tokens per request, your effective token compute drops accordingly.
[03:36] Samira: Let me show a table. Example request: 100 tokens decode, 900 tokens prefix. If KV cache hits for the 900 prefix 60% of the time, you only decode 100 + 360 effective tokens on average, not 1000. So cost ~64% lower for compute.
[03:58] Michael: That seems large; what's the impact on latency? caching trades compute for memory and potentially a cache lookup, right?
[04:10] Samira: Cache lookup is tiny (sub-ms) compared to model forward. Memory overhead is the main tradeoff — KV entries scale with context length and number of unique prefixes. For high cardinality prefixes you need eviction policies. We support LRU eviction and size-based TTLs.

[04:32] Jordan: What's the operational cost — do we need dedicated GPUs to host the KV store?
[04:38] Alex: No, KV cache sits in the runtime memory of the inference servers; if you use Dedicated you control pool size for memory capacity. For hosted, we manage it and provide config knobs. For your traffic pattern, we estimate needing ~200GB of additional KV storage across nodes if hit targets are high — which maps to an a few extra GPU nodes on Dedicated. We'll include that in the cost sheet.

[05:02] Samira: Also consider hybrid: prefix caching for common system+user templates (high reuse) and KV caching for sessions where history is large and reused across requests. Prefix cache is cheaper to store (hashed strings) and easier to evict.

[05:22] Alex: Now about batching & cache combined: caching increases effective batch density because cached prefixes reduce decode tokens, so throughput goes up and per-token cost drops. But if batches wait longer to fill, p95 can suffer, so we recommend per-route p95 caps as earlier.

[05:42] Michael: Any real numbers from customers?
[05:45] Samira: Yes — a retail recommendation customer saw a 55% token compute reduction and ~40% overall cost reduction after moving to KV prefix caching + dynamic batching. YMMV.

[06:00] Priya: On the cost model spreadsheet, what assumptions do you put in?
[06:04] Alex: We include model cost (per-token), infra amortized GPU per-hour, memory footprint for KV, expected hit rates, and batch size / latency tradeoffs. We'll share the sheet but for planning assume conservative hit rates (25-40%) initially.

[06:20] Samira: I'll call out the key parameters you'll want to provide: distribution of request lengths, percent of requests with repeatable prefixes, session reuse patterns, and desired latency SLOs. With traces we can run a simulation to recommend batch targets, cache sizes, and expected cost delta.

[06:40] Jordan: We have compliance questions — SOC2, customer-managed KMS, audit trails — how does Redwood handle that for Private?
[06:48] Alex: For Private we integrate with your KMS/HSM, full audit logs, RBAC and SSO. Hosted also supports tenant level encryption and SOC2 reports — we'll attach the SOC2 summary.

[07:05] Michael: What's the difference in pricing for dedicated vs hosted for this use case?
[07:10] Alex: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity/commit with lower unit costs but monthly commit. For heavy steady throughput, Dedicated with reserved GPU pools and our batching+cache profiles usually wins on cost. We'll model both options in the spreadsheet.

[07:30] Samira: Quick demonstration — I'm going to paste a simulation snippet. (screen share noises) Here we simulate 100k requests/day, average full tokens 800, cacheable prefix 600, and run 3 hit rate scenarios: 20%, 50%, 80%. At 50% hit rate and batch size 8 we show ~47% compute reduction and 35% net cost reduction after accounting for memory overhead.

[07:58] Priya: The memory overhead there is shown as 180GB in the sim, is that per-region?
[08:05] Samira: It's total cluster memory across inference nodes; per-region depends on your deployment topology. We'll break that out.

[08:18] Michael: OK — for pilot we'd want to start with a 1-week test against production traffic but with a limited percentage, like 5-10%. Is that doable?
[08:25] Alex: Yes, we typically do a pilot with shadowing and A/B. Samira can help configure a canary route and run benchmarks.

[08:34] Samira: For the pilot we'll need traces + expected success metrics (p95, throughput, token costs). We'll also need a list of routes to include.

[08:42] Jordan: About cache invalidation — if user updates profile, how do we ensure stale prefixes don't leak?
[08:49] Samira: You can attach TTLs or issue explicit invalidation calls via the control API; we support per-key TTL and versioned keys. Also the rollout can start with short TTLs to be safe.

[09:03] Michael: Can Redwood integrate with our feature store for keyed invalidation?
[09:07] Samira: Yes, we've integrated with common stores and you can push invalidation events to our control plane. For Private you can host the control plane internally.

[09:18] Priya: Any caveats with quantized models? we run int8 for cost reasons.
[09:22] Samira: Quantization reduces memory and compute but cache formats are the same; however INT8 variants may change kernel perf. Our runtime selects kernels accordingly; we'll note quantization in the cost sim.

[09:36] Alex: Let's surface example config we'll send: per-route batch target, max wait, cache type (prefix vs kv), TTL, eviction policy, and estimated memory footprint and cost delta.

[09:50] Alex: Quick pause — any further burning questions?
[09:53] Michael: One — how do you measure cache hit rate in production?
[09:57] Samira: We emit metrics: cache_hits, cache_misses, avg_kv_size, ttl_evictions, and per-route hit_rate. These appear in Redwood Console for observability.

[10:08] Priya: Ok that helps. Also want to see tracing at token level for debugging.
[10:12] Samira: We have token-level tracing hooks (sampling by request id) and a tracer UI you can enable.

[10:22] Alex: Alright, quick recap and next steps: We'll send the cost spreadsheet and an initial config template; Samira will scope the pilot and schedule the benchmark; Mike will share traces and acceptance criteria.

[10:35] Jordan: timeline wise we'd like results within 2-3 weeks.
[10:38] Alex: Totally reasonable. We'll aim for pilot kickoff next week.

[10:44] Michael: Thanks — this was helpful.

[10:47] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the sheet and SOC2 docs.

[10:52] End meeting.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional word swaps (e.g., "K-V cache" vs "KV cache"), speaker overlap at a few points, some numbers rounded in speech.
